title: Structured action contracts + runtime guardrails demo - Cerulean Systems
summary: Redwood AE/SE team walked Cerulean through a hands-on demo of structured action contracts (JSON mode), how to declare schemas for tool outputs, and runtime guardrails including automatic fallback to safe model variants and orchestration policies. Customer asked about encryption, RBAC, and latency/cost tradeoffs; SE ran a small live example invoking an external ticketing tool via function call and showed schema validation + automatic retry/fallback behavior.

Provide security whitepaper and SOC2 audit log sample - Kenji to share link
Schedule 1-week pilot spike with 50k tokens/day test profile - Dana/Ravi to confirm internal timeline
Run short benchmark for 128-token latencies from their GCP region - Luca to coordinate

transcript:
[00:00] Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, really appreciate you making time. Today we want to show JSON mode and how you can enforce action contracts, then drill into runtime guardrails and the Console Optimize suggestions.
[00:14] Dana (Head of ML): Yep thanks, excited — our main thing is we need safe tool calls for ticket creation and also strict schema outputs for our downstream processors.
[00:28] Luca (SE): Great, we'll start with a short slide... um, real quick context, Cerulean told us earlier you run a microservice for support tickets and you want to have LLM draft the payload and call the service programmatically?
[00:40] Ravi (VP Eng): Yeah, exactly. Ideally the LLM returns a JSON body we can POST to our existing API. We can't have random fields or wrong types.
[00:51] Sofia (Security): Also, encryption at rest and audit logs are a hard requirement. And the data residency question; we run in GCP europe-west1.
[01:04] Maya: Totally, we'll show how Redwood handles key things: schema enforcement in JSON mode, validators, and the fallback policy where if a response fails schema validation we can automatically run a repair pass or route to a safe model.
[01:20] Kenji (Solutions Eng): Quick note on pricing tradeoffs — stronger guardrails sometimes add 1-2ms per token for validation and optional repair, and can increase cost if you do extra completion passes. We'll show Optimize suggestions to tune batching and caching.
[01:35] Tom (SRE): Sounds good. On the security front, can we keep logs but redact sensitive fields?
[01:41] Priya (Product): Yes, Console has token-level cost/latency plus redaction hooks; you can configure patterns to mask PII before it lands in long-term logs.
[01:50] Luca: Ok starting the demo — I'm in the Console. First, JSON mode: we declare an output schema for the ticket payload. Example fields: title (string), priority (enum low|medium|high), customer_id (string), metadata (object with keys we allow), and an actions array for follow-ups.
[02:10] Luca: I'm pasting a schema now — you'll see the newer schema editor does inline validation. One common gotcha: if you define enums but the model writes a similar token like "high-priority" the validator will reject.
[02:25] Alicia (Frontend Eng): Wait can the validator auto-correct or suggest a mapping?
[02:29] Luca: Yes — there are three strategies: reject, repair (run a constrained completion to map values), or coerce (simple normalization). Repair means an extra completion call, so cost goes up a bit but you get deterministic output.
[02:43] Maya: We're going to demo a live flow where a user message creates a ticket, the model returns JSON, Redwood validates, and on failure we show the repair path and then the function call to the ticketing API.
[02:56] [demo noise, screen share change]
[03:05] Luca: Here's the prompt. I'm asking the model to: summarize the customer issue and generate a ticket. Switching to JSON mode now.
[03:15] [00:03] model: {"title":"Login fails - 500 error","priority":"high","customer_id":"C-1422","metadata":{"browser":"chrome"},"actions":[{"type":"assign","assignee":"support_team"}]}
[03:26] Luca: That passes schema validation. Now I'll change the sample input to produce an ambiguous priority like "really urgent".
[03:35] [00:05] model: {"title":"Payment flow broken","priority":"really urgent","customer_id":"C-332","metadata":{},"actions":[]}
[03:45] Luca: Validator marked that as invalid against the enum. Console shows the repair strategy — I pick 'repair' not 'reject'. Redwood issues a constrained completion to map "really urgent" -> "high".
[03:59] [03:59] model (repair pass): {"title":"Payment flow broken","priority":"high","customer_id":"C-332","metadata":{},"actions":[]}
[04:12] Maya: Now we demonstrate function calling: Redwood can call your downstream POST endpoint via a secure connector. I'm wiring a mocked ticket API.
[04:23] [04:23] Luca: We're invoking the function with the validated payload — note the Console shows schema and diff with the original.
[04:31] [04:31] function call result: 201 Created {"ticket_id":"T-9001"}
[04:40] Ravi: If the function call fails (e.g., 500), can Redwood automatically retry or fallback to a queued mode?
[04:47] Kenji: Yes — you can configure an orchestration policy: immediate retry x3 with exponential backoff, then queue to durable store and alert SRE. You can also choose to return a safe human-review action instead of failing silently.
[04:59] Sofia: For audit and compliance, do we get a full trace showing the original model output, the validator diff, and the function request/response?
[05:07] Priya: Yes, Console stores the chain: prompt, model outputs, validation results, repair completions, and outbound calls. You can configure retention and redaction settings.
[05:18] Dana: Good. Our other big concern is latency — most tickets are created synchronously in the UI and users won't wait 2 seconds. What's realistic for a repair pass?
[05:27] Luca: In our hosted tier a repair pass typically adds 100–300ms for a short 16–64 token mapping. For dedicated it's lower and for private on-prem you can tune the latency by colocating cache and model. If you use the 'coerce' strategy (simple rules) it's sub-50ms.
[05:45] Tom: OK. Can we run the logic so that the UI returns immediately with a provisional ticket and then confirm later?
[05:51] Maya: Yes — Redwood supports async patterns: you can return a provisional response and then update after the background workflow completes. We usually recommend that for UX-sensitive flows.
[06:00] [06:00] Luca: Switching to the Optimize panel — this is where we show recommendations to reduce token cost: set batching for similar requests, reuse prompt prefixes with caching, and quantization suggestions for model variants.
[06:14] Luca: For example, we see your workload is dominated by small ticket summaries; Optimize suggests a smaller model with a checkpointed cache and prefix caching, plus enabling automatic prefix/KV caching which reduces repeated context.
[06:29] Dana: If we pick the smaller model, how do we guard for hallucinations in the ticket body?
[06:33] Maya: Combine lower-cost model with stronger schema enforcement and a selective rerank step — rerank only when confidence is low. Also set up quality monitoring: we can run prompt-based evals and alert regressions.
[06:46] Ravi: Let's talk about private deployment. We may want on-prem for certain EU customers. How integrated is the same Console?
[06:55] Kenji: Same Console, separate control plane. Private deployment supports VPC peering, HSM/KMS integrations for keys, and audit export. There are small differences in available managed features but the API surface is identical.
[07:09] Sofia: For KMS, do you require us to manage keys or can Redwood manage?
[07:13] Priya: Both — you can bring-your-own-KMS or use Redwood-managed keys. For enterprise we recommend BYOK in HSM for the highest assurance.
[07:22] [07:22] Alicia: Back to tool calling: can Redwood call internal microservices behind our firewall?
[07:28] Kenji: With Private or Dedicated + Connector you can route calls over a secure tunnel or use a customer-managed NAT; the function connector runs in your VPC so it has internal access.
[07:37] Dana: Ok cool. Can we show a deeper technical example — Luca you mentioned fallback model variants earlier?
[07:43] Luca: Sure — I'll show a policy that picks the cheapest compatible model but has an SLO window: if latency spikes or validation fails repeatedly, it routes to a more capable variant or returns a human-review action.
[07:56] [07:56] Luca (typing): policy: prefer gpt-small-q4 -> if validation_fail_rate>1% or p95_latency>350ms then route to gpt-medium-q4 with canary for 10% traffic.
[08:11] Dana: That looks useful. How do we observe these metrics?
[08:14] Priya: Per-model and per-route dashboards in Console show p50/p95 latencies, validation failure rates, token cost, and downstream errors. You can set alerts on thresholds.
[08:24] Tom: On retention — we need audit logs for 1 year and data residency in eu-west1. Is retention configurable?
[08:31] Kenji: Yes, retention windows and where logs are stored are configurable per account. For EU residency the private control plane ensures logs remain in-region.
[08:41] [08:41] Ravi: Any caveats on the function connector? For example, how do credentials get rotated?
[08:46] Maya: The connector supports vault integrations; you can provide a service identity and we rotate tokens on a schedule or you can tie rotation to your KMS.
[08:54] Dana: Let's talk about a POC: our success criteria would be <200ms median ticket creation from our UI when using provisional response + background validation, less than 0.5% validation failure after repair, and a cost per ticket under $0.01. Can Redwood meet those?
[09:12] Luca: Based on the profile you gave, yes, likely on Dedicated. We'll run a 2-week pilot with traffic replay to measure exact numbers.
[09:20] Maya: Next steps we'll send a pricing estimate, security docs, and a proposed pilot plan.
[09:26] [09:26] Sofia: Quick question — do you support SAML SSO and role-based access?
[09:31] Priya: Yes SAML/SSO, SCIM provisioning, RBAC granular roles. We can demo the admin flow in a follow-up.
[09:38] Dana: Great. Anything else?
[09:41] Maya: We'll also include a short how-to for mapping nonstandard priority text to enum values and sample prompt templates.
[09:48] Ravi: OK please include that.
[09:51] [09:51] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the docs and pricing.
[09:56] [end of recording — approximate]
